claim: Over 200 different SARS-CoV-2 lineages have been observed in Mexico by November 2021.
source: Over 200 different SARS-CoV-2 lineages have been observed in Mexico by November 2021.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without supporting data or citations in the immediate context.

claim: Lineages B.1.1.222 and B.1.1.519 exhibited similar dynamics, constituting clades that likely originated in Mexico and persisted for >12 months.
source: Lineages B.1.1.222 and B.1.1.519 exhibited similar dynamics, constituting clades that likely originated in Mexico and persisted for >12 months.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylodynamic analysis results presented in the manuscript, including inferred MRCA dates and locations.

claim: Lineages B.1.1.7, P.1 and B.1.617.2 displayed similar dynamics, characterized by multiple introduction events leading to a few successful extended local transmission chains that persisted for several months.
source: Lineages B.1.1.7, P.1 and B.1.617.2 also displayed similar dynamics, characterized by multiple introduction events leading to a few successful extended local transmission chains that persisted for several months.
evidence: This is supported by phylodynamic analyses quantifying introduction events and identifying extended transmission chains in the Results section.

claim: Many clades were located within the south region of the country, suggesting that this area played a key role in the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Mexico.
source: Many clades were located within the south region of the country, suggesting that this area played a key role in the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Mexico.
evidence: This is supported by phylogeographic analyses showing clade distributions and viral diffusion patterns from southern states.

claim: Genome sequencing efforts for the surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 has granted public access to a massive number of virus genomes generated worldwide.
source: Genome sequencing efforts for the surveillance of the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) has granted public access to a massive number of virus genomes generated worldwide (https://www.gisaid.org/).
evidence: This is supported by reference to GISAID database and is common knowledge in the field.

claim: Exploring SARS-CoV-2 genome data using genomic epidemiology has allowed researchers to characterize increasing virus diversity.
source: Exploring SARS-CoV-2 genome data using genomic epidemiology has allowed researchers to characterize increasing virus diversity (Hill et al., 2021), track emerging viral subpopulations, and explore virus evolution in real-time, both at local and global scales (for examples see Kraemer et al., 2021; du Plessis et al., 2021; Worobey et al., 2020; Candido et al., 2020; COVID-19 Genomics UK (COG-UK) consortiumcontact@cogconsortium.uk, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Viral variants have emerged and circulated across different regions of the world throughout the development of the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: Throughout the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, viral variants have emerged and circulated across different regions of the world (Kraemer et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021), displaying specific mutations that define their phylogenetic patterns (Li et al., 2021; Tao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The emergence and spread of SARS-CoV-2 lineages has been routinely monitored since early 2021, informing public health authorities on their responses to the ongoing pandemic.
source: The emergence and spread of SARS-CoV-2 lineages has been routinely monitored since early 2021, informing public health authorities on their responses to the ongoing pandemic (Oude Munnink and Koopmans, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Emerging virus lineages are classified using a dynamic nomenclature system called the 'Pango system'.
source: Emerging virus lineages are classified using a dynamic nomenclature system ('Pango system', Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak Lineages), developed to consistently assign newly generated genomes to existing lineages, and to designate novel virus lineages according to their phylogenetic identity and epidemiological relevance (Rambaut et al., 2020; Ruis and Colquhoun, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original nomenclature system publications.

claim: Virus lineages that may pose an increased risk to global health have been classified as Variants of Interest (VOI), Variants under Monitoring (VUM), and Variants of Concern (VOC).
source: Virus lineages that may pose an increased risk to global health have been classified as Variants of Interest (VOI), Variants under Monitoring (VUM), and Variants of Concern (VOC), potentially displaying one or more of the following biological properties (Tao et al., 2021; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2022): increased transmissibility (Horby et al., 2021), decreasing the effectiveness of available diagnostics or therapeutic agents (such as monoclonal antibodies) (Weisblum et al., 2020), and evasion of immune responses (including vaccine-derived immunity) (Oude Munnink and Koopmans, 2023; Greaney et al., 2021a; Greaney et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research and public health guidelines.

claim: Five SARS-CoV-2 lineages have been designated as VOC: B.1.1.7 (Alpha), B.1.351 (Beta), P.1 (Gamma), B.1.617.2 (Delta), and B.1.1.529 (Omicron).
source: Up to date, five SARS-CoV-2 lineages (including all descending sub-lineages) have been designated as VOC: B.1.1.7 (Alpha), B.1.351 (Beta), P.1 (Gamma), B.1.617.2 (Delta), and B.1.1.529 (Omicron) (Oude Munnink and Koopmans, 2023; World Health Organization, 2021; O'Toole et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to WHO and published research.

claim: Virus lineages that dominate across various geographic regions are likely to have an evolutionary advantage, driven in part by a genetic increase in virus fitness.
source: Virus lineages that dominate across various geographic regions are likely to have an evolutionary advantage, driven in part by a genetic increase in virus fitness (i.e. mutations enhancing transmissibility and/or immune escape; Martin et al., 2021; Escalera-Zamudio et al., 2023; Kumar et al., 2021; Vöhringer et al., 2021; Caniels et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on viral fitness and evolution.

claim: The spread of different VOC across the world has been linked to human movement, often resulting in the replacement of previously dominating virus lineages.
source: Moreover, the spread of different VOC across the world has been linked to human movement, often resulting in the replacement of previously dominating virus lineages (Oude Munnink and Koopmans, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Exploring lineage replacement/fitness dynamics remains a challenge, as these are impacted by numerous factors.
source: However, exploring lineage replacement/fitness dynamics remains a challenge, as these are impacted by numerous factors, including differential and stochastic growth rates that vary across geographic regions, a shifting immune structure of the host population (linked to viral pre-exposure levels and vaccination rates), (Vöhringer et al., 2021; Caniels et al., 2021) and changing social behaviours (such as fluctuating human mobility patterns and the implementation of local non-pharmaceutical interventions across time) (Vöhringer et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020; Boutin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research discussing these factors.

claim: Mexico has been severely impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic, evidenced by a high number of cumulative deaths relative to other countries in Latin America.
source: Mexico has been severely impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic, evidenced by a high number of cumulative deaths relative to other countries in Latin America (Sánchez-Talanquer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The local epidemiological curve in Mexico fluctuated between three waves of infection observed in July 2020, January 2021, and August 2021.
source: Since the first introductions of the virus in early 2020 and up to November 2021 (Taboada et al., 2020), the local epidemiological curve fluctuated between three waves of infection (observed in July 2020, January 2021, and August 2021; Sánchez-Talanquer et al., 2021; Taboada et al., 2020; Ritchie, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and epidemiological data.

claim: Non-pharmaceutical interventions were implemented at a national scale in Mexico from March 23, 2020 to May 30, 2020.
source: Prior to the first peak of infection, non-pharmaceutical interventions (including social distancing and suspension of non-essential activities) were implemented at a national scale from March 23, 2020 to May 30, 2020.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about public health policy implementation.

claim: A reopening plan for Mexico was announced in May 13, 2020.
source: Nonetheless, a reopening plan for the country was already announced in May 13, 2020, whilst the national vaccination campaign did not begin before December 2020 (Sánchez-Talanquer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The national vaccination campaign in Mexico did not begin before December 2020.
source: Nonetheless, a reopening plan for the country was already announced in May 13, 2020, whilst the national vaccination campaign did not begin before December 2020 (Sánchez-Talanquer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The 'Mexican Consortium for Genomic Surveillance' (CoViGen-Mex) was launched in February 2021.
source: The 'Mexican Consortium for Genomic Surveillance' (abbreviated CoViGen-Mex) Consorcio de Vigilancia Genómica MexCoV2, 2021a was launched in February 2021, establishing systematic sequencing effort for a genomic epidemiology-based surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 in Mexico.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the establishment of the consortium.

claim: CoViGen-Mex aimed to sequence per month approximately 1200 representative samples derived from positive cases recorded throughout national territory.
source: In close collaboration with the national ministry of health, and driven by the sequencing capacity in the country, the program aimed to sequence per month approximately 1200 representative samples derived from positive cases recorded throughout national territory, based on the proportion of cases reported across states.
evidence: This describes the stated goals of the surveillance program.

claim: In May 2021, the sequencing scheme was upgraded to follow the official case report line.
source: In May 2021, the sequencing scheme was upgraded to follow the official case report line, in order to better coordinate case reporting and genome sampling across the country.
evidence: This describes a change in the surveillance program methodology.

claim: Over 48,000 viral genomes from Mexico were available from 2020 to 2021, resulting in an approximate average of 2000 viral genomes sequenced per month.
source: Derived from publicly accessible genome data from Mexico deposited in GISAID (https://www.gisaid.org/) from 2020 to 2021 (corresponding to the first year of the epidemic), over 48,000 viral genomes were available, resulting in an approximate average of 2000 viral genomes sequenced per month.
evidence: This is based on data from GISAID database.

claim: Starting February 2021, the CoViGen-Mex sampling scheme gradually increased its sequencing output from a mean of less than 500 genomes per month to over 1000 genomes from May 2021 onwards.
source: However, starting February 2021, the CoViGen-Mex sampling scheme gradually increased its sequencing output from a mean of less than 500 genomes per month to over 1000 genomes from May 2021 onwards.
evidence: This describes the sequencing output trends over time.

claim: Around 80,000 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Mexico were available in GISAID at the time of writing.
source: As of the time of writing this manuscript, around 80,000 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Mexico were available in GISAID, with one-third of these generated by CoViGen-Mex Consorcio de Vigilancia Genómica MexCoV2, 2021a (and other national institutions sequencing the rest).
evidence: This is based on data from GISAID database.

claim: Approximately 95% of all SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Mexico were generated in the country and 5% in the USA.
source: From these, approximately 95% of all SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Mexico were generated in the country and 5% in the USA.
evidence: This is based on metadata from GISAID database.

claim: During the first year of the epidemic in Mexico, over 200 different virus lineages were detected, including all VOCs.
source: During the first year of the epidemic in Mexico, over 200 different virus lineages were detected, including all VOCs O'Toole et al., 2021a; Consorcio de Vigilancia Genómica MexCoV2, 2021b.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published reports.

claim: Various virus lineages co-circulated across the national territory in Mexico.
source: Various virus lineages co-circulated across the national territory, a noteworthy observation in light of recombinant SARS-CoV-2 lineages that emerged in North America during 2021 (Gutierrez et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on recombinant lineages.

claim: Some virus lineages displayed specific dominance and replacement patterns that differed from those observed in neighboring countries, specifically the USA.
source: Additionally, some virus lineages displayed specific dominance and replacement patterns that differed from those observed in neighboring countries, specifically the USA (Consorcio de Vigilancia Genómica MexCoV2, 2021a; Consejo Nacional de Humanidades, Ciencias y Tecnologías, 2021; Taboada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published reports.

claim: The study investigated the introduction, spread, and replacement dynamics of five virus lineages: B.1.1.222, B.1.1.519, B.1.1.7 (VOC Alpha), P.1 (VOC Gamma), and B.1.617.2 (VOC Delta).
source: To achieve this, we investigated the introduction, spread, and replacement dynamics of five virus lineages that dominated during the first year of the epidemic: B.1.1.222, B.1.1.519, B.1.1.7 (VOC Alpha), P.1 (VOC Gamma), and B.1.617.2 (VOC Delta) (Consorcio de Vigilancia Genómica MexCoV2, 2021a; Consejo Nacional de Humanidades, Ciencias y Tecnologías, 2021; Taboada et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the study design and is supported by citations.

claim: The study used a phylodynamic approach to analyze publicly available cumulative SARS-CoV-2 genome data from Mexico in the context of virus genome data collected worldwide.
source: We used a phylodynamic approach to analyze publicly available cumulative SARS-CoV-2 genome data from the country in the context of virus genome data collected worldwide.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The study devised a human migration and phylogenetic-informed subsampling approach to increase the robustness of phylogeographic analyses.
source: We also devised a human migration and phylogenetic-informed subsampling approach to increase the robustness of our tailored phylogeographic analyses.
evidence: This describes a methodological innovation in the study.

claim: The study contrasted phylodynamic results with epidemiological and human mobility data.
source: To investigate lineage-specific spatial epidemiology, we contrasted our phylodynamic results with epidemiological and human mobility data, focusing on quantifying lineage importations into Mexico and characterizing local extended transmission chains across geographic regions (i.e. states).
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: B.1.1.222 and B.1.1.519 lineages likely originated in Mexico and denoted single extended transmission chains sustained for over a year.
source: Our analysis revealed similar dynamics for the B.1.1.222 and B.1.1.519 lineages, with both likely originating in Mexico and denoting single extended transmission chains sustained for over a year.
evidence: This is supported by phylodynamic analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: For P.1, B.1.1.7, and B.1.617.2 lineages, multiple introduction events were identified, with the detection of a few large transmission chains across the country.
source: For P.1, B.1.1.7, and B.1.617.2 lineages, multiple introduction events were identified, with the detection of a few large transmission chains across the country.
evidence: This is supported by phylodynamic analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: For B.1.617.2, a within-the-country virus diffusion pattern seeding from the south with subsequent movement into the central and north was observed.
source: For B.1.617.2, which represented the largest and most genetically diverse clades identified, we observed a within-the-country virus diffusion pattern seeding from the south with subsequent movement into the central and north.
evidence: This is supported by phylogeographic analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mexico's southern border may have played an important role in the introduction and spread of SARS-CoV-2 across the country.
source: We further identify Mexico's southern border may have played an important role in the introduction and spread of SARS-CoV-2 (and other epidemics) across the country.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogeographic patterns observed in the study.

claim: The sampling date of the study comprises January 2020 to November 2021, corresponding to the first year of the epidemic in Mexico.
source: The sampling date of this study comprises January 2020 to November 2021, corresponding to the first year of the epidemic in Mexico, just before the introduction of 'Omicron' (B.1.1.529) into the country (Consorcio de Vigilancia Genómica MexCoV2, 2021a; Consejo Nacional de Humanidades, Ciencias y Tecnologías, 2021; Taboada et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the temporal scope of the study and is supported by citations.

claim: During the study period, Mexico reported a daily mean test rate ranging between 0.13–0.18 test per 1,000 inhabitants.
source: During this time, Mexico reported a daily mean test rate ranging between 0.13–0.18 test per 1,000 inhabitants (Ritchie, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published data.

claim: The cumulative number of viral genomes generated throughout 2020 and 2021 correlates with the number of cases recorded at a national scale, corresponding to approximately 100 viral genomes per 10,000 cases, or ~1% of the official COVID-19 cases.
source: Despite a lower testing rate compared to other countries, the cumulative number of viral genomes generated throughout 2020 and 2021 (both by CoViGen-Mex and other national institutions) correlates with the number of cases recorded at a national scale, corresponding to approximately 100 viral genomes per 10,000 cases, or ~1% of the official COVID-19 cases (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and visualization in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 sequencing in Mexico remained centralized to Mexico City.
source: Although SARS-CoV-2 sequencing remained centralized to Mexico City, the proportion of viral genomes per state roughly coincided with the spatial distribution of confirmed cases (with Mexico City reporting most cases), as stated officially Informe Técnico Diario COVID-19 MÉXICO, 2021 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the sequencing infrastructure and is supported by data visualization.

claim: The proportion of viral genomes per state roughly coincided with the spatial distribution of confirmed cases.
source: Although SARS-CoV-2 sequencing remained centralized to Mexico City, the proportion of viral genomes per state roughly coincided with the spatial distribution of confirmed cases (with Mexico City reporting most cases), as stated officially Informe Técnico Diario COVID-19 MÉXICO, 2021 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and visualization in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 sequencing in Mexico has been sufficient to explore the spatial and temporal frequency of viral lineages across national territory.
source: Therefore, SARS-CoV-2 sequencing in Mexico has been sufficient to explore the spatial and temporal frequency of viral lineages across national territory (Consorcio de Vigilancia Genómica MexCoV2, 2021a; Consejo Nacional de Humanidades, Ciencias y Tecnologías, 2021; Taboada et al., 2021), now to further investigate the number of lineage-specific introduction events, and to characterize the extension and geographic distribution of associated transmission chains under a genomic epidemiology approach, as presented in this study.
evidence: This is an assessment of the adequacy of the sequencing data, supported by citations.

claim: Only the B.1.1.222, B.1.1.519, B.1.1.7 (Alpha), P.1 (Gamma), and B.1.617.2 (Delta) lineages displayed a dominant prevalence pattern within Mexico.
source: Our comparative analysis on the temporal distribution of virus lineages in Mexico confirmed previous published observations (O'Toole et al., 2021a; Consejo Nacional de Humanidades, Ciencias y Tecnologías, 2021; Taboada et al., 2021) showing that relative to other virus lineages circulating at the time, only the B.1.1.222, B.1.1.519, B.1.1.7 (Alpha), P.1 (Gamma), and B.1.617.2 (Delta) lineages displayed a dominant prevalence pattern within the country.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and citations to previous reports.

claim: For most dominant lineages, peaks in genome sampling frequency often coincided with the epidemiological waves of infection recorded (except for B.1.1.7 and P.1).
source: Moreover, for most of these dominant lineages, peaks in genome sampling frequency (defined here as the proportion of viral genomes assigned to a specific lineage, relative to the proportion of viral genomes assigned to any other virus lineage in a given time point) often coincided with the epidemiological waves of infection recorded (except for B.1.1.7 and P.1) (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and visualization in Figure 1.

claim: The B.1.1.222 lineage circulated in North America between April 2020 and September 2021, mostly within the USA (~80%) and Mexico (~20%).
source: The B.1.1.222 lineage circulated in North America between April 2020 and September 2021, mostly within the USA (~80% of all B.1.1.222-assigned genomes) and Mexico (~20% of all B.1.1.222-assigned genomes).
evidence: This is based on analysis of genome data from GISAID.

claim: B.1.1.222 was considered as endemic to North America.
source: With limited reports from other regions of the world, B.1.1.222 was thus considered as endemic to the region (https://cov-lineages.org/) O'Toole et al., 2021b.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and reference to the cov-lineages database.

claim: The first B.1.1.222-assigned genome was sampled from Mexico on April 2020.
source: The first B.1.1.222-assigned genome was sampled from Mexico on April 2020 (Mexico/CMX-INER-0026/2020-04-04) O'Toole et al., 2021b, whilst the last B.1.1.222-assigned genome was sampled from the USA on September 2021 (USA/CA-CDPH-1002006730/2021-09-14).
evidence: This is based on genome data from GISAID and is supported by a citation.

claim: The latest sampling date for B.1.1.222 in Mexico corresponds to July 2021, two months before the latest sampling date of the lineage at an international scale.
source: The latest sampling date for B.1.1.222 in Mexico corresponds to July 2021 (Mexico/CHH_INER_IMSS_1674/2021-07-26), two months before the latest sampling date of the lineage at an international scale.
evidence: This is based on genome data from GISAID.

claim: In Mexico, the B.1.1.222 lineage was continuously detected between April 2020 and May 2021, followed by a steady decline after July 2021.
source: We observe that in Mexico, the B.1.1.222 lineage was continuously detected between April 2020 and May 2021, followed by a steady decline after July 2021 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and visualization in Figure 1b.

claim: During its circulation period, most B.1.1.222 genomes were collected from the central region of the country, represented by Mexico City.
source: During its circulation period, most B.1.1.222 genomes were collected from the central region of the country, represented by Mexico City (CMX; Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and visualization in Figure 2a.

claim: For B.1.1.222, a rising genome sampling frequency was observed from May 2020 onwards, coinciding with the first epidemiological wave recorded during July 2020.
source: For B.1.1.222, a rising genome sampling frequency was observed from May 2020 onwards, coinciding with the first epidemiological wave recorded during July 2020.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: B.1.1.222 genome sampling frequency progressively increased to reach a highest of 35% recorded in October 2020.
source: Subsequently, genome sampling frequency progressively increased to reach a highest of 35% recorded in October 2020, denoting established dominance before the emergence and spread of B.1.1.519 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and visualization in Figure 1b.

claim: Data from the first year of the epidemic initially revealed that the B.1.1.222 lineage had reached a maximum genome sampling frequency of approximately 10%.
source: Data from the first year of the epidemic (available until February 2021, as analyzed by Taboada et al., 2021; O'Toole et al., 2021a; Consejo Nacional de Humanidades, Ciencias y Tecnologías, 2021) initially revealed that the B.1.1.222 lineage had reached a maximum genome sampling frequency of approximately 10%.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous reports.

claim: The vast majority of B.1.1.222-assigned genomes from Mexico (>80%) were generated, assigned, and submitted to GISAID after February 2021.
source: However, our results show an important frequency underestimation (10% vs 35%), since the vast majority of B.1.1.222-assigned genomes from Mexico (>80%) were generated, assigned, and submitted to GISAID after February 2021.
evidence: This is based on analysis of genome submission dates in GISAID.

claim: In the USA, the B.1.1.222 lineage reached a maximum genome sampling frequency of 3.5%, compared to a 35% observed in Mexico.
source: Notably, in the USA, the B.1.1.222 lineage reached a maximum genome sampling frequency of 3.5%, compared to a 35% observed in Mexico.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of genome data from both countries.

claim: The four-fold difference in the number of B.1.1.222-assigned genomes between the USA and Mexico reflects a significant disparity in sequencing efforts between the two countries.
source: This four-fold difference in the number of B.1.1.222-assigned genomes between the USA and Mexico reflects a significant disparity in sequencing efforts between the two countries, and contrasts with region-specific epidemiological scenarios Hill et al., 2021.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative data analysis and is supported by a citation.

claim: Sequencing disparities and sampling gaps between countries can hinder the development of global outbreak control strategies and exacerbate existing health inequalities.
source: This is of great importance since sequencing disparities and sampling gaps between countries can hinder the development of global outbreak control strategies and exacerbate existing health inequalities.
evidence: This is a general statement about the implications of sequencing disparities.

claim: Phylodynamic analysis for the B.1.1.222 lineage revealed one main clade deriving from a single earliest MRCA with a 'most likely' location inferred to be 'Mexico' (PP: 0.99).
source: Phylodynamic analysis for the B.1.1.222 lineage revealed one main clade deriving from a single earliest MRCA (most recent common ancestor) with a 'most likely' location (supported by a relative Posterior Probability [PP] of 0.99) inferred to be 'Mexico', denoting lineage emergence in the country (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by phylodynamic analysis results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The inferred date for the B.1.1.222 MRCA corresponds to March 2020, denoting a cryptic circulation period of a month.
source: The inferred date for this MRCA corresponds to March 2020, further denoting a cryptic circulation period of a month (before the earliest sampling date for the lineage within the country, see Methods section "Time-scaled analysis").
evidence: This is based on phylodynamic analysis results.

claim: After emergence, B.1.1.222 was seeded into the USA from Mexico multiple times.
source: After emergence, B.1.1.222 was seeded into the USA from Mexico multiple times.
evidence: This is based on phylogeographic analysis results.

claim: A minimum of 237 introduction events from Mexico into the USA were estimated for B.1.1.222 (95% HPD interval = [225-250]).
source: In this context, we estimate a minimum of 237 introduction events from Mexico into the USA (95% HPD interval = [225-250]), and a minimum of 106 introduction events from the USA into Mexico (95% HPD interval = [93-120]; Figure 2a).
evidence: This is based on phylogeographic analysis results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A minimum of 106 introduction events from the USA into Mexico were estimated for B.1.1.222 (95% HPD interval = [93-120]).
source: In this context, we estimate a minimum of 237 introduction events from Mexico into the USA (95% HPD interval = [225-250]), and a minimum of 106 introduction events from the USA into Mexico (95% HPD interval = [93-120]; Figure 2a).
evidence: This is based on phylogeographic analysis results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Based on inferred node dates in the MCC tree, the B.1.1.222 lineage displayed a total persistence of up to 16 months.
source: Based on inferred node dates (for MRCAs) in the MCC tree, the B.1.1.222 lineage displayed a total persistence of up to 16 months.
evidence: This is based on phylodynamic analysis results.

claim: B.1.1.519 directly descended from B.1.1.222.
source: Directly descending from B.1.1.222 (Figure 1a), the B.1.1.519 lineage circulated in North America between August 2020 and November 2021, mostly within the USA (~60% of all B.1.1.519-assigned genomes) and Mexico (~30% of all B.1.1.519-assigned genomes).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The B.1.1.519 lineage circulated in North America between August 2020 and November 2021, mostly within the USA (~60%) and Mexico (~30%).
source: Directly descending from B.1.1.222 (Figure 1a), the B.1.1.519 lineage circulated in North America between August 2020 and November 2021, mostly within the USA (~60% of all B.1.1.519-assigned genomes) and Mexico (~30% of all B.1.1.519-assigned genomes).
evidence: This is based on analysis of genome data from GISAID.

claim: B.1.1.519 was considered as endemic to North America.
source: As for B.1.1.222, B.1.1.519 genome reporting from other countries was limited, and the B.1.1.519 lineage was also considered as endemic to the region (https://cov-lineages.org/) (Taboada et al., 2021; O'Toole et al., 2021l; Cedro-Tanda et al., 2021; Rodríguez-Maldonado et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to the cov-lineages database.

claim: The earliest B.1.1.519-assigned genome was sampled from the USA on July 2020.
source: At an international scale, the earliest B.1.1.519-assigned genome was sampled from the USA on July 2020 (USA/TX-HMH-MCoV-45579/2020-07-31) O'Toole et al., 2021c, whilst the latest B.1.1.519-assigned genome was sampled from Mexico on December 2021 (Mexico/CHP_IBT_IMSS_5310/2021-12-27) Aceves et al., 2021.
evidence: This is based on genome data from GISAID and is supported by a citation.

claim: The latest B.1.1.519-assigned genome was sampled from Mexico on December 2021.
source: At an international scale, the earliest B.1.1.519-assigned genome was sampled from the USA on July 2020 (USA/TX-HMH-MCoV-45579/2020-07-31) O'Toole et al., 2021c, whilst the latest B.1.1.519-assigned genome was sampled from Mexico on December 2021 (Mexico/CHP_IBT_IMSS_5310/2021-12-27) Aceves et al., 2021.
evidence: This is based on genome data from GISAID and is supported by a citation.

claim: Most B.1.1.519-assigned genomes collected after November 2021 came from outside North America and were identified as outliers within the tree, likely to be sequencing errors.
source: During initial phylogenetic assessment, we noted that most of B.1.1.519-assigned genomes collected after November 2021 came from outside North America (namely, from Turkey and Africa). These were further identified as outliers within the tree, likely to be sequencing errors resulting, and thus were excluded from further analyses.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and quality control procedures.

claim: In Mexico, the B.1.1.519 lineage was first detected on August 2020.
source: In Mexico, the B.1.1.519 lineage was first detected on August 2020 (Mexico/YUC-NYGC-39037-20/2020-08-28) (Taboada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on genome data and is supported by a citation.

claim: B.1.1.519 displayed an increasing genome sampling frequency observed between September 2020 and July 2021.
source: Our analysis derived from cumulative genome data from Mexico shows that B.1.1.519 displayed an increasing genome sampling frequency observed between September 2020 and July 2021 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and visualization in Figure 1b.

claim: Contrasting to C5d, C6d denotes an extended transmission chain with a geographic distribution mainly restricted to central Mexico.

claim: The MRCA of the C6d clade dates to April, displaying a clade persistence of seven months (from April 2021 to November 2021).

source: Well-supported transitions (scored under a BF >100 and a PP >.90) were mostly inferred from the southern state of Campeche (CAM) into central and northern states, and subsequently from the northern state of Chihuahua (CHH) into the central and northern region of the country, with some bidirectionality observed.

claim: Human movement can directly contribute to virus spread into unexposed areas.
source: Human movement can directly contribute to virus spread into unexposed areas, while mobility patterns may also reveal the impact of social and demographic factors on epidemics, such as population density and the effectiveness of non-pharmaceutical interventions at different scales.

claim: Tracking human mobility is crucial to understand virus spread, especially when other factors cannot fully explain observed trends.
source: Thus, tracking human mobility is crucial to understand virus spread, especially when other factors cannot fully explain observed trends.

claim: Human mobility data analysis revealed two mobility peaks across time in Mexico.

claim: The first mobility peak occurred between February and April 2021, coinciding with the introduction and spread of the B.1.1.7 and P.1+ lineages, and with the contraction of B.1.1.519.
source: The first occurred between February and April 2021, coinciding with the introduction and spread of the B.1.1.7 and P.1+lineages, and with the contraction of B.1.1.519.
evidence: This is based on analysis of human mobility data and viral lineage dynamics.

claim: The second mobility peak was observed between August and November 2021, coinciding with the expansion of the B.1.617.2 lineage.
source: The second mobility peak was observed between August and November 2021, coinciding with the expansion of the B.1.617.2 lineage.
evidence: This is based on analysis of human mobility data and viral lineage dynamics.

claim: Increased human movement were observed for Mexico City, and to a lesser extent, for Jalisco, the State of Mexico, Nuevo León and Puebla (followed by Coahuila, Guanajuato, and Veracruz).
source: Increased human movement (represented by the cumulative number of trips into a given state) were observed for Mexico City, and to a lesser extent, for Jalisco, the State of Mexico, Nuevo León and Puebla (followed by Coahuila, Guanajuato, and Veracruz; Figure 1c).
evidence: This is based on analysis of human mobility data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Mean connectivity within national territory revealed intensified movements from Mexico City into the State of Mexico, Morelos, Hidalgo, Puebla, Veracruz and Jalisco, and from Jalisco into Michoacán and Guadalajara.
source: Mean connectivity within national territory revealed intensified movements from Mexico City into the State of Mexico, Morelos, Hidalgo, Puebla, Veracruz and Jalisco, and from Jalisco into Michoacán and Guadalajara (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: For both the C5d and C6d clades, no correlation between viral transitions and mean connectivity was observed.
source: However, for both the C5d and C6d clades, no correlation between viral transitions and mean connectivity was observed (C5d: Adjusted R-squared: 0.006577, F-statistic: 7.15 on 1 and 928 DF, p-value: 0.007628. C6d: Adjusted R-squared: 0.3216, F-statistic: 470.8 on 1 and 990 DF, p-value:<2.2e-16), nor with the pairwise distance between states (C5d: Adjusted R-squared: 0.01086, F-statistic: 4.051 on 1 and 277 DF, p-value: 0.04511. C6d: Adjusted R-squared: 0.02296, F-statistic: 2.715 on 1 and 72 DF, p-value: 0.1038).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the relationship between viral transitions and mobility data.

claim: Many of the lineage-specific clades identified displayed a geographic distribution within southern region of the country (i.e. clades C3a and C7 for B.1.1.7, clade C1_P1_17 for P.1, and clades C2d and C5d for B.1.617.2).
source: Many of the lineage-specific clades we identify displayed a geographic distribution within southern region of the country (i.e. clades C3a and C7 for B.1.1.7, clade C1_P1_17 for P.1, and clades C2d and C5d for B.1.617.2).

claim: Ranking connectivity between the southern region of the country (represented by Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Chiapas and Campeche) and the remaining 28 states revealed a consistently high number of bidirectional movements between regions.
source: In this context, ranking connectivity between the southern region of the country (represented by Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Chiapas and Campeche) and the remaining 28 states did reveal a consistently high number of bidirectional movements between regions (represented by the CAM, CMX, and VER; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of human mobility data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both the B.1.1.222 and B.1.1.519 lineages likely originated in Mexico, characterized by single clades denoting extended sustained transmission for over a year.
source: Our results reveal contrasting epidemiological and evolutionary dynamics between virus lineages circulating in Mexico during the first year of the epidemic, with some identifiable patterns. Both the B.1.1.222 and B.1.1.519 lineages likely originated in Mexico, characterized by single clades denoting extended sustained transmission for over a year.
evidence: This is a summary of phylodynamic analysis results.

claim: During their circulation, both B.1.1.222 and B.1.1.519 lineages dominated in Mexico, and were seeded back and forth between Mexico and the USA, but never dominated across the USA.
source: During this time, both lineages dominated in Mexico, and were seeded back and forth between Mexico and the USA, but never dominated across the USA.
evidence: This is based on phylogeographic analysis results and comparative data analysis.

claim: The number of publicly available viral genomes from each country reflects sequencing disparities that contrast with the lineage-specific epidemiological patterns observed across regions.
source: Thus, the number of publicly available viral genomes from each country reflects sequencing disparities that contrast with the lineage-specific epidemiological patterns observed across regions, highlighting the need to leverage genomic surveillance efforts across neighboring nations using joint strategies (Hill et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative data analysis and is supported by a citation.

claim: Peaks in P.1 and B.1.1.7 genome sampling frequencies coincided with a decrease in cases following the second wave of infection.
source: Further similarities were observed for the P.1 and B.1.1.7 lineages, for which peaks in genome sampling frequencies coincided with a decrease in cases following the second wave of infection.
evidence: This is based on data analysis of genome sampling frequencies and epidemiological data.

claim: P.1 and B.1.1.7 did not dominate in Mexico, in contrast to what was observed in other countries such as the UK and USA.
source: We further confirm that P.1 and B.1.1.7 did not dominate in Mexico Taboada et al., 2021; Zárate et al., 2022, in contrast to what was observed in other countries such as the UK and USA (Vöhringer et al., 2021; Faria et al., 2021; Washington et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and citations to published research.

claim: Similar observations regarding B.1.1.7 dynamics were independently made for other Latin American countries, suggesting that the overall epidemiological dynamics of B.1.1.7 in Latin America may have differed substantially from that observed in the USA and UK.
source: Similar observations were independently made for other Latin American countries (some with better genome representation than others, like Brazil Faria et al., 2021), suggesting that the overall epidemiological dynamics of B.1.1.7 in Latin America may have differed substantially from that observed in the USA and UK (Vöhringer et al., 2021; Faria et al., 2021; Washington et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative data analysis and is supported by citations.

claim: Differences in B.1.1.7 dynamics could be explained partly by competition between lineages, exemplified in Mexico by the regional co-circulation of B.1.1.7, P.1, and B.1.1.519.
source: Such differences could be explained partly by competition between lineages, exemplified in Mexico by the regional co-circulation of B.1.1.7, P.1, and B.1.1.519.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on observed lineage dynamics.

source: Nonetheless, a lack of representative number of viral genomes for most of these countries prevents exploring such hypothesis at a larger scale, and further highlights the need to strengthen genomic epidemiology-based surveillance.
evidence: This is a statement about data limitations.

claim: The overall evolutionary dynamics observed for B.1.1.7, P.1, and B.1.617.2 VOC are comparable to those reported in other countries.
source: However, the overall evolutionary dynamics observed for these VOC are comparable to those reported in other countries (Vöhringer et al., 2021; Faria et al., 2021; Washington et al., 2021).

source: As an example, in the USA, the earliest introductions reported for the B.1.1.7 lineage were synchronous to those observed in Mexico (occurring between October and November 2020) and were also characterized by a few extended transmissions chains with a distribution often constrained to specific states (Washington et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

source: Thus, as drawn from our study, the successful spread of a given virus lineage does not seem to be linked to a higher number of introduction events, but rather to the extent and distribution of transmission chains, with size likely reflecting virus transmissibility (Grenfell et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the study results and is supported by a citation.

claim: In Mexico, the introduction and spread of the B.1.1.7, P.1, and B.1.617.2 lineages was characterized by multiple introduction events, resulting in a few successful extended local transmission chains.
source: In Mexico, the introduction and spread of the B.1.1.7, P.1, and B.1.617.2 lineages was characterized by multiple introduction events, resulting in a few successful extended local transmission chains.

source: The epidemiological and evolutionary dynamics of the three VOC show that not only did these coincide temporally, but also revealed multiple and independent transmission chains corresponding to different lineages (and sub-lineages) spreading across the same geographic regions.

claim: Several clades belonging to different virus lineages were distributed within the south region of the country, suggesting that this area has played a key role in the spread of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Our results further revealed several clades belonging to different virus lineages distributed within the south region of the country, suggesting that this area has played a key role in the spread of SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogeographic analysis results.

source: Of notice, such pattern is comparable to what has been observed for arboviral epidemics in Mexico (Gutierrez et al., 2023; Thézé et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on arboviral epidemics.

claim: Common epidemiological patterns between SARS-CoV-2 and arboviruses may have emerged in Mexico due to the dependence of vector populations on human behavior and mobility patterns.
source: Despite differences in the transmission mechanism between SARS-CoV-2 and arboviruses, we speculate that common epidemiological patterns may have emerged in Mexico due to the dependence of vector populations on human behavior and mobility patterns (Gutierrez et al., 2023; Thézé et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations.

claim: Virus transmission rates may vary within specific regions due to population density coupled with social factors (for example, unregulated migration across borders).
source: Virus transmission rates may also vary within specific regions due to population density coupled with social factors (for example, unregulated migration across borders).
evidence: This is a general statement about factors affecting virus transmission.

claim: The southern region of Mexico (represented by Chiapas, Yucatán, and Quintana Roo) may be a common virus entry and seeding point.
source: Jointly, these observations indicate that the southern region of Mexico (represented by the states of Chiapas, Yucatán, and Quintana Roo) may be a common virus entry and seeding point, emphasising the need for an enhanced virus surveillance in states that share borders with neighboring countries, and highlights the importance of devising social behavior-informed tailored surveillance strategies applied to specific states (i.e. sub-region-specific surveillance).

claim: An increasing growth rate (Rt) observed for different SARS-CoV-2 lineages dominating across specific regions can be partially explained by a fluctuating virus genetic background (i.e. emerging mutations that impact viral fitness).
source: In general, an increasing growth rate (Rt; defined as the instantaneous reproductive number that measures how an infection multiplies Royal Statistical Society, 2021) observed for different SARS-CoV-2 lineages dominating across specific regions can be partially explained by a fluctuating virus genetic background (i.e. emerging mutations that impact viral fitness) (Vöhringer et al., 2021; Faria et al., 2021; Washington et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

source: In light of our results, relative to the parental B.1.1.222 lineage, B.1.1.519 displayed only two amino acid changes within the Spike protein: T478K and P681H (Rodríguez-Maldonado et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mutation T478K locates within the Receptor Binding Domain (RBD), with a potential impact in antibody-mediated neutralization.
source: Mutation T478K locates within the Receptor Binding Domain (RBD), with a potential impact in antibody-mediated neutralization (Liu et al., 2021; Wilhelm et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

source: Thus, it may enhance virus entry (Lubinski et al., 2021), reduce antibody-mediated recognition (Haynes et al., 2021), and confer Type I interferon resistance (Lista et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: At least one of the mutations (T478K or P681H) may have contributed to the dominance of B.1.1.519 over B.1.1.222 by increasing the Rt.
source: We speculate that at least one of these mutations may have contributed to the dominance of B.1.1.519 over B.1.1.222 by increasing the Rt, as has been observed for other SARS-CoV-2 subpopulations (Martin et al., 2021; Escalera-Zamudio et al., 2023; Dolan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations.

source: Notably, the mutations observed for B.1.1.519 were not exclusive to the lineage, as P681H emerged later and independently in B.1.1.7 (and to a lesser extent in P.1, corresponding to 5% of all sampled genomes) (Naveca et al., 2021; Hodcroft, 2021b), whilst mutation T478K subsequently appeared in B.1.617.2 (Liu et al., 2021; Lubinski et al., 2021; Lista et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Data derived from the natural virus population evidences amino acid changes at site 681 of the Spike protein have been predominantly fixed in VOC, with some mutations likely to yield an evolutionary advantage.
source: Although assessing the impact of emerging mutations on lineage-specific fitness requires experimental validation, data derived from the natural virus population evidences amino acid changes at site 681 of the Spike protein have been predominantly fixed in VOC, with some mutations likely to yield an evolutionary advantage (Liu et al., 2021; Lubinski et al., 2021; Lista et al., 2021; Hodcroft and Neher, 2021; Pond, 2021; Hodcroft, 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: A somewhat 'shared' genetic background between the B.1.1.519 and B.1.1.7 lineages (as represented by mutation P681H) may have limited the spread of B.1.1.7 across Mexico.
source: Thus, we propose that a somewhat 'shared' genetic background between the B.1.1.519 and B.1.1.7 lineages (as represented by mutation P681H) may have limited the spread of B.1.1.7 across the country.

source: In Mexico, relatively widespread and constant exposure levels to genetically similar virus subpopulations for extended periods of time (represented by the B.1.1.222 and B.1.1.519 lineages) may have yielded consistently increasing immunity levels in a somewhat still naïve population (with a nationwide seroprevalence of ~33.5% estimated by December 2020 Basto-Abreu et al., 2022; Muñoz-Medina et al., 2021).

source: As more genetically divergent virus lineages were introduced and began to spread across the country (represented by B.1.1.7 and P.1, and later by B.1.617.2), a shift in the local immune landscape is likely to have occurred, impacted by a viral genetic background prompting (a partial) evasion of the existing immune responses.

claim: A vaccination rate of above 50% was only reached after December 2021 in Mexico.
source: Supporting this observation, a vaccination rate of above 50% was only reached after December 2021 (Ritchie, 2020; Bhatia et al., 2020), suggesting that immunity levels during the first year of the epidemic mostly depended on virus pre-exposure levels.

claim: Immunity levels during the first year of the epidemic in Mexico mostly depended on virus pre-exposure levels.
source: Supporting this observation, a vaccination rate of above 50% was only reached after December 2021 (Ritchie, 2020; Bhatia et al., 2020), suggesting that immunity levels during the first year of the epidemic mostly depended on virus pre-exposure levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on vaccination data.

claim: The fluctuating mobility patterns observed for Mexico were consistent with a decrease in cases following the second and third waves of infection, likely reflecting changes in the color-coded system regulating travel restrictions.
source: In the context of human movement related to the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Mexico, the fluctuating mobility patterns we observed for the country were consistent with a decrease in cases following the second and third waves of infection, likely reflecting changes in the color-coded system regulating travel restrictions leveraged by the risk of infection (Gobierno de México, 2021b).
evidence: This is an inference based on mobility data analysis and is supported by a citation.

claim: The geographic distances and overall human mobility trends observed within Mexico did not correlate with the virus diffusion patterns inferred (represented by B.1.617.2).
source: However, contrasting to our expectations on viral diffusion processes to be associated with local human mobility patterns, the geographic distances and overall human mobility trends observed within Mexico did not correlate with the virus diffusion patterns inferred (represented by B.1.617.2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the relationship between mobility and viral diffusion.

claim: As geographic distances and human mobility cannot be considered potential predictors of SARS-CoV-2 spread in Mexico, viral diffusion could be explained (to some extent) by human movement across borders.
source: As geographic distances and human mobility cannot be considered potential predictors of SARS-CoV-2 spread in Mexico, viral diffusion could be explained (to some extent) by human movement across borders.

claim: It has been proposed that the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Mexico is linked to human mobility across USA.
source: Taking this into consideration, it has been proposed that the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Mexico is linked to human mobility across USA (for example, see Zárate et al., 2022), as we further evidence in this study by the transmission patterns observed for the B.1.1.222 and the B.1.1.519 lineages at an international scale.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and by the study's own results.

claim: Some of the virus diffusion patterns observed are congruent with human migration routes from South and Central America.
source: However, some of the virus diffusion patterns we observed are also congruent with human migration routes from South and Central America, supporting the notion that SARS-CoV-2 spread in Mexico has been impacted by epidemics within neighboring regions, and further underlines the need to investigate the potential role of irregular migration on virus spread across geographic regions (Kraemer et al., 2020b; IOM Global Migration Data Analysis Centre, 2021; Varela Huerta, 2018; París-Pombo, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogeographic patterns and is supported by citations.

claim: Limitations of the study include uncertainty in determining source locations for virus introduction events into the country (for most lineages), restricted by regional genome sampling biases.
source: Limitations of our study include uncertainty in determining source locations for virus introduction events into the country (for most lineages), restricted by regional genome sampling biases (Kalkauskas et al., 2021; De Maio et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about study limitations supported by citations.

claim: Study limitations are further impacted by (i) an uneven genome sampling across foreign locations and within the country, and (ii) by a poor viral genome representation for many countries in Central and South America.
source: This is further impacted by (i) an uneven genome sampling across foreign locations and within the country, and (ii) by a poor viral genome representation for many countries in Central and South America (GISAID, 2008; Gutierrez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about study limitations supported by citations.

claim: Sampling biases are likely to affect the viral diffusion reconstructions presented, likely rendering them incomplete.
source: Such biases are also likely to affect the viral diffusion reconstructions we present, likely rendering them incomplete.
evidence: This is a statement about study limitations.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 genome sampling and sequencing in Mexico has been sufficient to robustly quantify and characterize lineage-specific transmission chains.
source: However, as SARS-CoV-2 genome sampling and sequencing in Mexico has been sufficient, we are still able to robustly quantify and characterize lineage-specific transmission chains.

claim: A differential proportion of cumulative viral genomes sequenced per state does not necessarily mirror the geographic distribution and extension of the transmission chains identified, but rather represents a fluctuating intensity in virus genome sampling and sequencing through time.
source: It is worth highlighting that a differential proportion of cumulative viral genomes sequenced per state does not necessarily mirror the geographic distribution and extension of the transmission chains identified, but rather represents a fluctuating intensity in virus genome sampling and sequencing through time.

source: A more homogeneous sampling across the country is unlikely to impact our main findings, but could (i) help pinpoint additional clades we are currently unable to detect, (ii) provide further details on the geographic distribution of clades across other regions of the country, and (iii) deliver a higher resolution for the viral spread reconstructions we present.

claim: The study prompts the need to better understand the impact of land-based migration across national borders, and encourages joint virus surveillance efforts in the Americas.
source: Overall, our study prompts the need to better understand the impact of land-based migration across national borders, and encourages joint virus surveillance efforts in the Americas.
